correctness.rationale: For every \(m\ge1\), use exact discriminant of \(z^m-a\) and pairwise resultants to reduce the squared evaluation determinant to equation (1). An exhaustive parameterization of unordered two-point phase configurations reduces the product of outer distances to a strictly convex quadratic in the mean-phase cosine, thereby proving its globally optimal antipodal mean. The remaining scalar objective \((1-t^2)(A-Bt)^2\) has exactly one maximum on \([-1,0]\), at the displayed negative quadratic root. Boundary half-gap degeneracy is strictly inferior. The exact radical and strict comparison were checked algebraically, including the symbolic \(m=2\) determinant, and 30 direct finite determinant instances plus ten independent global numerical optimizations. The proof, not finite search, establishes the universal quantifiers. The limit uses \(q=(r/s)^m\to0\) and \(mq\to0\). No assumptions are made about conditioning.

The close Hardy result concerns the Gram of d normalized Szegő kernels at same-radius Blaschke zeros; setting d=3m does not yield our determinant because its Cauchy denominator is nonconstant and its allowed radii are all equal. The classical Vandermonde factorization is credited; the new implication is its nontrivial strict two-radius global optimization and exponential asymptotic improvement.

value.rationale: The geometry is a natural D-optimal design problem in finite Hardy polynomial interpolation: choosing two inner orbit phase offsets changes the product of all singular values and hence the sampling-volume amplification. The closed radical classifies the unique optimum for every orbit size and radius pair, and proves that the naive regular stagger fails for every strict radial contrast. The relative squared determinant advantage is \((4/3)^m(1+o(1))\), exponentially large with orbit size at fixed radial ratio, and not merely a tiny numerical improvement. The result gives a precise angular prescription applicable before computing an interpolation inverse, while explicitly not claiming improved worst-case singular value.
